questions.q: A server sends a page's HTML once. How can JavaScript make a new task appear on that page without reloading it?
questions.explain: The browser parses the HTML once into the DOM and draws from that tree. Changing the tree changes the screen. The original HTML text is never read again.
options: By editing the HTML text the server sent, which the browser re-reads after every change
By changing the DOM, the tree of objects the browser built from the HTML and draws the screen from
By sending the new HTML back to the server, which pushes an updated page
By calling document.write, the only way to add content after load

questions.q: For this HTML, what are list.childNodes.length and list.children.length?
questions.explain: childNodes includes the whitespace text nodes: one before the first li, one between them, one after the last. That is 3 text nodes plus 2 elements. children counts only elements.
options: 2 and 2
5 and 2
3 and 2
2 and 5

questions.q: What happens when this runs on a page that has no element with the id total?
questions.explain: querySelector returns null when nothing matches, and setting a property on null throws a TypeError. For elements the page needs, check for null and throw an error that names the selector.
options: Nothing: the assignment is ignored
A new element with id total is created
A TypeError is thrown, because querySelector returned null
querySelector throws a NotFoundError before the assignment

questions.q: Which of these returns a live collection that changes when elements are added to or removed from the page?
questions.explain: getElementsByClassName and getElementsByTagName return live HTMLCollections. querySelectorAll returns a static snapshot, and copying any collection into an array also freezes it.
options: document.querySelectorAll(".task")
document.getElementsByClassName("task")
[...document.querySelectorAll(".task")]
Array.from(document.getElementsByClassName("task"))

questions.q: The HTML is indented as usual (<ul>, a line break, then two spaces and the first <li>). Why does ul.firstChild.textContent not give the first task's title?
questions.explain: Line breaks and indentation between tags become text nodes. The …Element… properties (firstElementChild, nextElementSibling) skip them.
options: Because firstChild returns the last child
Because firstChild is the whitespace text node before the first <li>; firstElementChild is the <li>
Because textContent does not work on list items
Because the browser removes the first child while parsing

questions.q: A task title comes from a user. Which line puts it on the page safely?
questions.explain: textContent always treats the string as text. The other three parse it as HTML, so a title containing an element with an event-handler attribute runs the attacker's code: XSS.
options: li.innerHTML = title;
li.innerHTML = `<span>${title}</span>`;
li.textContent = title;
li.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", title);

questions.q: A colleague says: "innerHTML is safe for user text, because a <script> inserted with it never runs." What is wrong with that?
questions.explain: The lesson's example put <img src="data:," onerror="…"> in a title: the image failed to load and the onerror code ran. Attackers have many ways to run code without <script>.
options: Nothing: without script tags, no code can run
Scripts inserted with innerHTML do run, in every browser
Event-handler attributes such as onerror on an inserted <img> do run, so an attacker does not need a script tag
It is only unsafe in old browsers

questions.q: The HTML says <input name="title" value="Buy detergent">. The user types "Buy gloves". What do input.value and input.getAttribute("value") return?
questions.explain: The attribute is the default value from the HTML; the property is the current value. Typing changes only the property. Read user input from value.
options: "Buy gloves" and "Buy gloves"
"Buy gloves" and "Buy detergent"
"Buy detergent" and "Buy gloves"
"Buy detergent" and "Buy detergent"

questions.q: What does summary.setAttribute("hidden", "false") do?
questions.explain: Boolean attributes (hidden, disabled, checked) are on when present. To switch one off, set the property to false or call removeAttribute.
options: Shows the element, because the value is "false"
Hides the element: a boolean attribute is on whenever it is present, whatever its value
Throws, because hidden only accepts true
Nothing, because attributes and properties are unrelated

questions.q: A list has three tasks. What does list.append(list.firstElementChild) do?
questions.explain: A node can only be in one place. Inserting a node that is already in the tree moves it. Use cloneNode(true) when you want a copy.
options: Adds a copy of the first task at the end, so there are four
Moves the first task to the end; there are still three
Throws, because the element is already in the list
Does nothing, because the element is already a child of list

questions.q: A row has data-id="2" and the tasks array has { id: 2, … }. Why does tasks.find((t) => t.id === row.dataset.id) return undefined?
questions.explain: Attribute values, and therefore dataset values, are always strings. Convert with Number(row.dataset.id) before comparing.
options: dataset only works for ids above 9
The attribute should be named data-Id
dataset.id is the string "2", and 2 === "2" is false
find cannot be used on arrays of objects

questions.q: What is a DocumentFragment good for?
questions.explain: A fragment is a container node that is not in the page. Appending it moves all of its children into the page at once: one change instead of one per item.
options: Storing a part of the page in localStorage
Splitting a large document into several pages
Building many nodes off the page and inserting them all in one operation, which leaves the fragment empty
Keeping a copy of elements that were removed

questions.q: Which statement about a <template> element is true?
questions.explain: template.content is a DocumentFragment outside the page. Clone it (cloneNode(true)) for each row and fill the data in with textContent.
options: Its content is shown on the page until JavaScript hides it
Scripts and images inside it run and load as soon as the page loads
Its content is parsed but not shown or searched by document.querySelectorAll; you clone template.content to use it
It can only contain text, not elements

questions.q: A plain <script> in the <head> runs document.querySelector("#tasks") and gets null, although #tasks is in the body. What is the best fix?
questions.explain: The browser runs a plain script as soon as it reaches it, before it has parsed the rest of the page. Deferred and module scripts run after parsing, in order.
options: Call querySelector in a loop until it finds the element
Load the script with defer (or as type="module") so it runs after the HTML is parsed
Use getElementById, which also searches elements not parsed yet
Wrap the call in try/catch

questions.q: A form is inside main. The user has typed in its input. Then this runs: main.innerHTML += "<p>Draft saved</p>". What happens to the input?
questions.explain: += reads the whole inside as a string, appends to it, and parses it again into new elements. The old ones, with everything that lived only on them, are thrown away.
options: Nothing: only the new paragraph is added
It is replaced by a new input built from the HTML, so the typed text, focus and listeners are lost
The typed text is kept, but the listeners are lost
The input is duplicated

questions.q: Why does the task list keep its tasks in an array and call render() after every change, instead of adding and counting <li> elements directly?
questions.explain: When the DOM is the data, each change must update every place that depends on it, and one forgotten place (like the summary) makes the page lie. Rendering from state makes the page a function of the data.
options: Because arrays are faster than DOM elements to draw
So there is one source of truth: every part of the page, list and summary alike, is drawn from the same data and cannot disagree
Because the DOM cannot store more than a few hundred elements
Because render() keeps focus and scroll position automatically

questions.q: What is the most useful thing a test of the task list checks?
questions.explain: Tests that read the page like a user survive refactoring. Tools like jsdom (a DOM in Node) and Testing Library (find by text and role) are built for exactly that.
options: That render was called exactly once per action
The private variables inside render
What a user would see: the row titles, which checkboxes are ticked, and the summary text, read back from the page
The exact CSS class names on every element

questions.q: Which loop is likely to make the browser recalculate the layout many times?
questions.explain: Reading a layout property after a change forces the browser to calculate layout right then. Alternating reads and writes does that once per row (layout thrashing). Read everything first, then write everything, as in B.
options: A: each turn reads layout (offsetHeight) right after the previous turn changed it
B: it loops over the rows twice
Both equally
Neither: browsers only calculate layout when the page is drawn

questions.q: Why should a "Delete" action be a <button> rather than a <div> with a click listener?
questions.explain: Using the element that means what you want gives you keyboard support, focus and correct screen-reader behaviour. The lesson also gave each button an aria-label naming its task.
options: A <div> cannot have a click listener
A button can be reached and pressed with the keyboard and is announced as a button by screen readers; a div gets none of that for free
Buttons render faster
A <div> cannot contain text

questions.q: A profile page shows a link to the user's website with a.setAttribute("href", user.website). What must you still check?
questions.explain: setAttribute does not parse HTML, so it is safe from tag injection, but some attributes run code by design. Parse the URL (new URL) and allow only the protocols you expect.
options: Nothing: setAttribute escapes the value
That the URL is shorter than 2,000 characters
That the address starts with http: or https:, because a javascript: URL runs code when the link is clicked
That the URL is written in lower case

questions.q: Why does every element have an addEventListener method?
questions.explain: An <li> is an HTMLLIElement → HTMLElement → Element → Node → EventTarget. Methods live on those prototypes and are shared by every element.
options: Because the browser copies it onto every element when the page loads
Because every element's prototype chain ends in Node and then EventTarget, which defines it
Because it is a global function
Because HTMLElement is a subclass of Function

questions.q: When would you use innerText instead of textContent?
questions.explain: innerText follows CSS, so it must ask for an up-to-date layout. textContent just returns all the text nodes' text, which is faster and what you want most of the time. Both are safe for setting text.
options: Always: it is the modern replacement
When setting user text safely; textContent is not safe
When you want the text as the user sees it (hidden parts left out, line breaks from the layout), accepting that it is slower because it needs layout
When the element contains HTML you want parsed

questions.q: This escapeHtml has its replacements in a different order from the lesson's. What does it print?
questions.explain: The last step replaces every &, including the ones the first two steps just wrote, so < becomes &lt;. A browser would show the entity text instead of a <. Escape & first.
options: &amp;lt;b&amp;gt;Tea &amp; cake&amp;lt;/b&amp;gt;
&lt;b&gt;Tea &amp; cake&lt;/b&gt;
&lt;b&gt;Tea & cake&lt;/b&gt;
<b>Tea &amp; cake</b>

questions.q: With the lesson's escapeHtml (which escapes & first), what does this print?
questions.explain: Text that already looks like an entity is still just text, so its & is escaped and the page shows < literally, exactly as the user typed it. String(text) turns the number into "42" first.
options:
5 &amp;lt; 6
42

5 &lt; 6
42

5 &amp;lt; 6
TypeError: text.replaceAll is not a function

questions.q: This array behaves like a live collection: removing an item shrinks it while the loop runs. What does it print?
questions.explain: Removing index 0 shifts "Pay bill" to index 0, but i moves on to 1 and skips it. Every second item survives. This is exactly the bug with a live HTMLCollection; loop over a static snapshot instead.
options: [ 'Pay bill', 'Order mops' ]
[ 'Buy detergent', 'Clean flat' ]
[ 'Order mops' ]

questions.q: dataset turns data-* attribute names into property names. This function does the same conversion. What does it print?
questions.explain: Each dash followed by a lower-case letter becomes that letter in upper case, which is how data-due-date becomes dataset.dueDate. The g flag replaces every match, not only the first.
questions.code:
const toCamel = (name) => name.replace(/-([a-z])/g, (_, c) => c.toUpperCase());
console.log(toCamel("due-date"), toCamel("id"), toCamel("customer-full-name"));
options: dueDate id customerFullName
due-date id customer-full-name
DueDate Id CustomerFullName
dueDate id customerFull-name

questions.q: This plain object models an indented <ul> the way the DOM stores it. What does it print?
questions.explain: The whitespace between tags is kept as text nodes, so there are 5 child nodes but only 2 element children, and the first child is a line break plus indentation.
options:
2 2
"Buy detergent"

questions.q: The summary is computed once and stored, like text written into the DOM. What does this print?
questions.explain: What is on the page does not update itself when the data changes. Only calling render() again brings it up to date. The new task is done, so the open count stays 1.
options:
1 of 1 tasks left
1 of 2 tasks left

1 of 2 tasks left
1 of 2 tasks left

1 of 1 tasks left
2 of 2 tasks left

1 of 1 tasks left
1 of 1 tasks left

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Values from data-* attributes are strings, and === does not convert, so 2 === "2" is false. Converting with Number first finds the task.
options:
undefined
Pay bill

{ id: 2, title: 'Pay bill' }
Pay bill

undefined
undefined

{ id: 2, title: 'Pay bill' }
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'title')

questions.q: This closest walks up parent links, like Element.closest. What does it print?
questions.explain: The search starts at the node itself, so closest(li, "li") finds li. The li has no id, so ?? falls back to its tag. No ancestor is a form, so the loop ends and returns null.
options: li tasks null li
li tasks null null
li ul null li
undefined tasks null li

questions.q: Boolean attributes are on when present. This models that rule with an object of attributes. What does it print?
questions.explain: Only presence counts. hidden="false" and hidden="" are both present, so both are on. That is why the lesson sets the hidden property instead.
options: true false true
false false true
false false false
true false false

questions.q: Moving an item in an array works like appending an element that is already in the page. What does it print?
questions.explain: The item is taken out of its old place and put at the end, so the length stays 3. splice and push change the original array, so list itself is now in the new order.
options: Pay bill | Clean flat | Buy detergent 3
Buy detergent | Pay bill | Clean flat | Buy detergent 4
Pay bill | Clean flat | Buy detergent 4
Buy detergent | Pay bill | Clean flat 3

questions.q: An href property is the attribute resolved against the page's base URL, which is what new URL(value, base) does. What does this print?
questions.explain: A relative path is resolved from the base's folder (/app/); a path starting with / starts from the root of the site; .. goes up one folder. getAttribute("href") would return the unresolved text instead.
options:
https://tasks.example/app/jobs/2026?view=list
https://tasks.example/jobs
/help

https://tasks.example/jobs/2026?view=list
https://tasks.example/app/jobs
/app/help

jobs/2026?view=list
/jobs
../help

https://tasks.example/app/jobs/2026?view=list
https://tasks.example/app/jobs

questions.explain: Done tasks get [x], titles are trimmed, and only the one task that is not done counts as open.
options:
[x] Buy detergent
[ ] Pay bill
1 of 2 tasks left

[x]  Buy detergent

questions.q: Write escapeHtml(text) that makes any value safe to put inside HTML: convert it to a string, then replace &, <, >, " and ' with &, <, >, " and ', in an order that never escapes twice.
questions.explain: & goes first, so the ampersands written by the later replacements are not escaped again. On a page, prefer textContent; escaping is for places where you must build HTML text.

questions.q: li.dataset.dueDate = "…" writes the attribute data-due-date. Write dataAttributeName(key) that turns a dataset key into its attribute name: each upper-case letter becomes a dash plus the lower-case letter, and data- goes in front.
questions.explain: A regular expression with the g flag finds every capital letter, and the replacement function returns a dash and the lower-case letter. This is the reverse of how the browser builds dataset property names.

questions.q: Write summaryText(tasks) for the task list's summary line. It counts the tasks that are not done and returns "No tasks left" for 0, "1 task left" for 1, and "N tasks left" otherwise.
questions.explain: Keep this logic in a pure function that returns a string. render() then only does summary.textContent = summaryText(state.tasks), and the wording can be tested without a page. For many languages, Intl.PluralRules picks the right plural form.
questions.expected:
No tasks left
1 task left
2 tasks left

questions.q: Nodes here are plain objects with tag, optional id and parent. Write closest(node, tag) that returns the first node, starting with node itself and going up through parent, whose tag matches, or null. Print the ids it finds.
questions.explain: The walk begins with the node itself, which is why closest(button, "button") finds the button. When it runs past the root (parent is null) nothing matched. Element.closest works the same way, with a CSS selector instead of a tag.

questions.q: A tree of plain objects models the DOM: element nodes have tag and childNodes, text nodes have text. Write a recursive countElements(node) that counts the element nodes, including node itself, and ignores text nodes.
questions.explain: A text node is the base case and counts 0. An element counts 1 plus whatever its children count: main, h1, ul, two li and one b make 6. The lesson's walk function used the same recursion on the real DOM.

questions.q: Write textContent(node) for the same kind of object tree: a text node returns its text; an element returns the text of all its children joined together, in order. Print the text of the list.
questions.explain: This is how the DOM's textContent getter behaves: it concatenates every text node inside the element, at any depth, and ignores the tags.

questions.q: For a safe highlighter, split a title into parts: plain strings, and objects { mark: "…" } for each case-insensitive match of term. Leave out empty strings. An empty term means no matches. (A DOM version would turn strings into text nodes and marks into <mark> elements.)
questions.explain: Searching a lower-case copy finds matches in any capitalisation, while slicing the original keeps the user's letters. Nothing is ever parsed as HTML, so the <b> in the title stays text. Without the empty-term check, indexOf("") would match at every position forever.

questions.q: Write checkTitle(raw) for new tasks. Trim the input. Return { error: "A task needs a title." } if nothing is left, { error: "Keep the title under 120 characters." } if it is longer than 120, and otherwise { title } with the trimmed title, unchanged (angle brackets are allowed).
questions.explain: Validation refuses what cannot be a task and keeps everything else exactly as typed. Angle brackets are legitimate text; making them safe is the job of the code that displays them (textContent), not of validation.
